Assignment 2 — Data Preparation & Baseline¶

Predicting failed public-procurement contracts in Kazakhstan¶

Author: Aziz Abdulin · Course project: Tender Risk ML · Repository: https://github.com/awzwz/tender-risk-ml

This notebook takes the raw open-data snapshot of the Kazakhstan public procurement portal and turns it into a clean, leakage-safe modelling table with a time-based train / validation / test split, followed by a first baseline model. It is organised in the order of the assessment criteria:

§ Criterion
1 Dataset selection and description
2 Research problem, research questions, hypotheses
3 Data loading & reproducibility
4 Data structure examination
5 Data quality assessment
6 Data cleaning (before → after)
7–8 Exploratory data analysis and visualisation
9 Features, target, data-leakage audit
10 Train / validation / test split
11 Baseline model
12 Scientific interpretation and conclusions

How to run: Kernel → Restart & Run All. The notebook finds the repository root by itself and downloads the data snapshot (≈400 MB, GitHub release data-v1) on first run if data/raw/ is empty. Full run ≈ 1–2 minutes. On Google Colab, run the commented cell in §3 first.

1. Dataset selection and description¶
Source OWS v3 GraphQL API of the Kazakhstan public procurement portal — the official open-data interface of goszakup.gov.kz, operated by the Ministry of Finance of the Republic of Kazakhstan. API: https://ows.goszakup.gov.kz · portal: https://goszakup.gov.kz
Domain Public procurement (government purchasing of goods, works and services)
Origin Administrative records created by the e-procurement system itself: every announcement, lot, supplier application and contract is registered electronically by the portal. Not a survey, not synthetic.
Collection Collected by the author between 12 September and 6 October 2026 with src/collect.py (resumable cursor pagination over the API, personal API token). Raw snapshot is published as GitHub release data-v1 so the analysis is reproducible without a token.
Period All procurements published 1 January – 31 March 2024 and every record linked to them (lots, applications, contracts), plus the full register of unreliable suppliers (RNU) as of October 2026.
Size 5 linked tables, ≈3.6 million rows, 400 MB in Parquet (details in §4).
Purpose of the dataset Transparency of state spending: the portal publishes it so that citizens, auditors and journalists can monitor procurement.

Why this dataset fits the task. The research task (§2) needs (a) a large number of independent purchasing decisions, (b) information available before the contract is executed, and (c) an observed outcome of the contract. This dataset provides all three: hundreds of thousands of procurements, their attributes and competition at award time, and the final legal status of every contract (executed / terminated / not concluded). Q1 2024 was chosen deliberately: by October 2026 every contract from that quarter has had more than two years to reach its final status, so the outcome label is settled rather than "still in progress".

2. Research problem¶

Problem. Kazakhstan's procurement portal handles ≈1.8 million procurements per year. A noticeable share of the resulting contracts are terminated or never signed, which means repeated procedures, delayed goods and services and wasted budget. Control bodies can inspect only a tiny fraction of procurements by hand, so they need a way to tell in advance which procurements are likely to end badly.

Research aim. To determine which characteristics of a procurement, known at the moment the winner is selected, are associated with the failure of the resulting contract, and whether these characteristics allow failures to be predicted on a later time period.

Research questions and hypotheses

Research question Hypothesis
RQ1 How are the procurement method and the level of competition (number of bidders) related to the probability that the contract fails? H1: within the same procurement method, single-bidder procurements fail more often than procurements with moderate competition (2–3 bidders).
RQ2 Is the failure probability associated with the size, type and location of the purchase (value; goods / works / services; region)? H2: the failure probability increases with the procurement value.
RQ3 Can information available at award time separate failing from successful contracts substantially better than chance on a later period? H3: a simple linear baseline trained on January–February 2024 reaches ROC-AUC well above 0.5 and a PR-AUC several times above the base rate on March 2024.

The outcome studied (target) is contract_failed — whether the contract that resulted from the procurement was terminated or not concluded (exact definition in §9).

All five tables load without errors. They are linked like tables of a relational database:

  • trd_buy.id ← lots.trdBuyId, contracts.trdBuyId, trd_app.buyId (procurement id is the foreign key);
  • rnu.supplierBiin ↔ contracts.supplierBiin (BIN — the business identification number of a company).

4.3 What the important columns mean¶

Table Column Meaning
trd_buy id, numberAnno technical id and public announcement number of the procurement
RefTradeMethods_nameRu procurement method: request for quotations, open tender, single source after a failed tender, framework agreement, …
refSubjectTypeId subject of the purchase: 1 = goods, 2 = works, 3 = services
totalSum planned value of the procurement, KZT
countLots number of lots in the announcement
publishDate, startDate, endDate publication date and the window during which suppliers may submit applications
kato location code (KATO classifier); its first two digits are the region
orgBin BIN of the organiser (the buying institution)
parentId link to an earlier procurement (set mostly for single-source purchases after a failed tender)
singlOrgSign, isConstructionWork, isLightIndustry, disablePersonId flags: single organiser, construction works, light industry, organisations of disabled people
lots amount, count planned total value and quantity of the lot
nameRu, descriptionRu catalogue name and description of what is bought (text)
dumping anti-dumping provisions apply to the lot (tenders only)
trd_app buyId, supplierBinIin which supplier applied to which procurement
AppLots JSON list of per-lot offers: lot id, unit price, status
contracts rootId, parentId a contract and all its amendments share the same rootId
refContractStatusId / RefContractStatus_nameRu legal status: executed, partially executed, terminated (unilaterally / by agreement), not concluded, amended, … — source of the target
contractSum, faktSum, faktExecDate contract value and actual execution — only known after execution
rnu supplierBiin, startDate, endDate supplier and period of inclusion in the register of unreliable suppliers

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
m = miss.assign(label=miss.table + "." + miss.column).set_index("label")["missing_%"].sort_values()
m.plot.barh(ax=ax, color=[PALETTE["fail"] if v == 100 else PALETTE["ok"] for v in m])

ax.set_xlabel("Missing values, % of rows")
ax.set_ylabel("table.column")
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter())
for i, v in enumerate(m):
    ax.text(v + 0.8, i, f"{v:.1f}%", va="center", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG / "fig01_missing.png", dpi=150); plt.show()

Interpretation (Figure 1). Missingness is concentrated in a few columns and is mostly structural, not random:

  • trd_buy.customerBin and trd_buy.customerNameRu are 100 % empty — the API never fills them for this entity (the customer is identified through orgBin and the lots instead). They carry no information and will be dropped.
  • trd_buy.biinSupplier / idSupplier (winner) are missing for ≈78 % of procurements — the winner is reliably recorded only in contracts, so we take it from there.
  • repeatStartDate/repeatEndDate exist only for repeated procedures — missing means "not repeated".
  • contracts.RefContractCancel (the id of the nested cancellation object) is also 100 % empty; its readable counterpart RefContractCancel_nameRu is filled only for the 2.3 % of contracts that were cancelled.
  • contracts.signDate is missing for 8.2 thousand rows (1.5 %); ≈ 7.5 thousand of them have the status Not concluded — the contract was never signed, so the gap is expected and confirms the status.
  • contracts.faktExecDate (actual execution date) is missing for 22 % of rows — contracts that were not (fully) executed — and contractEndDate is almost never filled (96 %); both describe the outcome and are not used as features.
  • trd_app.AppLots is missing for 181 applications (0.02 %) — applications without any lot offer.

There are no exact duplicates of records (every id is unique, business keys are unique). The one real duplication problem is semantic: 75,454 contract rows (13.6 %) are amendments — additional versions of an already existing contract that share its rootId. Treating them as separate contracts would count the same contract several times with different statuses; they are collapsed in §6. The only other anomaly is one RNU record without a supplier BIN.

Category labels are consistent in spelling, but the method variable has a long tail: 17 methods, of which 10 cover less than 0.5 % of procurements each, and several are near-duplicates by meaning ("Request for quotations" vs "Request for quotations (non-GZ new)"; "Single source after failed tenders" vs the same with "non-GZ"). Rare methods will be grouped into Other so that each category has enough observations.

    SELECT b.price * l.count / l.amount AS r

    WHERE b.price > 0 AND l.amount > 0 AND l.count > 0''').df().r

totalSum: median 242,589 KZT, max 79,843,399,986 KZT; skewness 210.9
IQR rule on log10 scale: 12,967 high and 2,214 low outliers (2.41%)

bid / planned unit price: median 0.791; > 1 (bid above planned price): 0.58%; < 0.05 (95 %+ below plan, implausible): 0.56%; max 100.0
  • Procurement value is extremely right-skewed (median ≈ 240 thousand KZT, maximum ≈ 80 billion KZT). The large values are real (construction, infrastructure), not errors, so they are kept and modelled on a log scale.
  • Bid-to-plan price ratio: by law an offer may not exceed the planned price, yet a small share of offers are above it, and some are 20× below it. These are unit-of-measure inconsistencies (e.g. the price entered per package while the plan is per item), so ratios outside [0.05, 1.0] are treated as invalid in §6.

5.5 Coverage of the RNU register (important for leakage)¶

In [16]:
r = raw["rnu"]
print("RNU inclusions by start year:", r.startDate.str[:4].value_counts().sort_index().to_dict())
print("RNU entries already active on 2024-01-01:", int(((r.startDate < "2024-01-01") & (r.endDate > "2024-01-01")).sum()))

RNU inclusions by start year: {'2024': 2707, '2025': 8682, '2026': 5954}
RNU entries already active on 2024-01-01: 0

The register only contains current entries (inclusions start in 2024–2026 and last two years; expired entries are removed by the portal). No supplier was in the register before our procurements, while many were added after them — very likely because of the terminated contracts we want to predict. RNU therefore cannot be used as a feature (it would leak the outcome); it is kept only for descriptive analysis.

The only remaining gaps are in the competition features: bids_per_lot / best_bid_ratio are undefined when no priced offer was recorded (flagged by no_bids), and bid_price_cv (price dispersion) is undefined when a lot had a single offer. They are not filled here: imputation is fitted on the training set only (inside the model pipeline, §11) to avoid leaking validation statistics into training.

Strict definition (without termination by mutual agreement): 4.51%
Partially executed (kept as 0, reported separately): 3.20%

Interpretation (Figure 2). About one procurement in fifteen (6.6 %) ends with a failed contract. The most common failure is unilateral termination (usually the customer terminating a supplier who does not deliver), followed by termination by agreement and contracts that were never signed. The classes are imbalanced 1 : 14, so accuracy would be a misleading metric (always predicting "not failed" is already 93 % accurate); the baseline is evaluated with ROC-AUC, PR-AUC and F1 instead.

Note: a pilot sample in the proposal (A1) suggested ≈ 23 %. The full data show the pilot was biased — it came from one page of the API ordered by id; the full population is the reliable estimate.

7.2 Procurement value¶

In [23]:
def rate_ci(g):
    p = g.mean(); n = len(g); se = np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
    return pd.Series({"rate": p, "lo": p - 1.96 * se, "hi": p + 1.96 * se, "n": n})

df["value_decile"] = pd.qcut(df.log_total_sum, 10, labels=False) + 1
dec = df.groupby("value_decile").contract_failed.apply(rate_ci).unstack()
dec["median_value"] = df.groupby("value_decile").total_sum.median()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.8))
ax.errorbar(dec.index, dec.rate * 100, yerr=[(dec.rate - dec.lo) * 100, (dec.hi - dec.rate) * 100],
            marker="o", color=PALETTE["fail"], capsize=3)
ax.axhline(y.mean() * 100, ls="--", color=PALETTE["grey"], label=f"overall rate {y.mean():.1%}")
ax.set_xticks(dec.index)
ax.set_xticklabels([f"D{i}\n{v / 1e3:,.0f}k" if v < 1e6 else f"D{i}\n{v / 1e6:,.1f}M" for i, v in dec.median_value.items()])
ax.set_title("Figure 3. Contract failure rate by procurement value decile (95 % CI)")
ax.set_xlabel("Value decile (median value of the decile, KZT)"); ax.set_ylabel("Failed contracts, %")
ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG / "fig03_value.png", dpi=150); plt.show()

Observation 1 (Figure 3). Failure risk rises almost monotonically and tenfold with procurement value: from ≈ 1.5 % in the cheapest decile (median 16 thousand KZT) to ≈ 16.5 % in the most expensive one (median ≈ 10 million KZT). The confidence intervals do not overlap between the lowest and highest deciles, so this is not noise. Large contracts are longer and more complex, give the supplier more room to fail, and make termination worthwhile for the customer. This supports H2.

7.3 Procurement method¶

ax.set_title("Figure 4. Contract failure rate by procurement method (95 % CI)")
ax.set_xlabel("Failed contracts, %"); ax.set_ylabel("Procurement method"); ax.set_xlim(0, meth.rate.max() * 100 * 1.5)
ax.legend(loc="lower right"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG / "fig04_method.png", dpi=150); plt.show()

Observation 2 (Figure 4). The method matters a lot. Requests for quotations — the cheapest, fastest procedure where the lowest price wins automatically — have the highest failure rate (≈ 9 %), while single-source purchases after a failed tender fail only ≈ 3 % of the time and framework-agreement call-offs ≈ 1 %. A plausible mechanism: automatic lowest-price selection attracts unrealistic offers that the winner later cannot honour, while in a single-source purchase the terms are negotiated with a supplier who has explicitly agreed to them, and framework call-offs go to pre-qualified suppliers.

Observation 3 (Figure 5) — Simpson's paradox. Looking at all procurements together, one bidder seems to be the safest situation (4.4 %). But half of single-bidder procurements are single-source purchases, which are low-risk for the reason shown in Figure 4. Within the same method the picture reverses: for requests for quotations a single bidder means ≈ 9.8 % failures versus ≈ 5.8 % with two bidders, and the same holds for open tenders. This supports H1 — but only once the method is controlled for, which is why the method must enter the model together with competition.

Observation 4. The relationship is U-shaped: with 6+ bidders the failure rate climbs back to ≈ 11 %. Fierce competition for lowest-price procedures pushes winners to bid below their real cost (the winner's curse), which later shows up as non-delivery. Procurements with no recorded offers but with a contract (mostly single-source) have the highest rate inside each method (≈ 17–18 %).

ax.set_title("By subject of purchase"); ax.set_xlabel("Subject"); ax.set_ylabel("Failed contracts, %")
ax.set_ylim(0, subj.rate.max() * 100 * 1.3)
ax = axes[1]
colors = [PALETTE["fail"] if r_ in ("Astana", "Almaty city", "Shymkent") else PALETTE["ok"] for r_ in reg.index]
ax.barh(reg.index, reg.rate * 100, xerr=[(reg.rate - reg.lo) * 100, (reg.hi - reg.rate) * 100], color=colors, capsize=2)
ax.axvline(y.mean() * 100, ls="--", color=PALETTE["grey"], label=f"overall {y.mean():.1%}")
ax.set_title("By region (red = cities of republican significance)"); ax.set_xlabel("Failed contracts, %"); ax.set_ylabel("")
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
fig.suptitle("Figure 6. Contract failure rate by subject of purchase and by region (95 % CI)", fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG / "fig06_subject_region.png", dpi=150); plt.show()

Observation 5 (Figure 6, left). Goods fail more than twice as often as services (≈ 9.1 % vs 4.2 %), with works in between (7.6 %). Services such as utilities, internet or cleaning are typically delivered by the same established providers every year, whereas goods depend on supply chains and price changes between bid and delivery.

Observation 6 (Figure 6, right). Regional differences are large and systematic: the three cities of republican significance — Astana (10.6 %), Shymkent (9.4 %) and Almaty (8.8 %) — have the highest failure rates, about twice the rate of West Kazakhstan, Kyzylorda or Pavlodar (≈ 5 %). Big cities have more suppliers and more competitive, lower-priced bidding, which is consistent with Observation 4. Region is therefore a useful feature (RQ2).

Observation 7 (Figure 7). Volume is highest in January (start of the budget year) and declines towards March, but the failure rate is stable at 6.4–6.8 % per month with no trend. The outcome-generating process does not drift within the quarter, which makes a chronological split (§10) a fair test: a model trained on January–February is evaluated on a period with the same base rate but unseen procurements.

7.7 Relationships between numeric features¶

In [28]:
num_cols = ["log_total_sum", "n_lots", "bid_window_days", "publish_to_start_days", "n_applications", "n_bidders",
            "bids_per_lot", "best_bid_ratio", "bid_price_cv", "org_prior_buys", "has_parent", "contract_failed"]
corr = df[num_cols].corr(method="spearman")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 8))
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="RdBu_r", center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1, ax=ax,
            cbar_kws={"label": "Spearman correlation"}, annot_kws={"size": 8})
ax.set_title("Figure 8. Spearman correlations between numeric features and the target")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG / "fig08_corr.png", dpi=150); plt.show()

Observation 8 (Figure 8). No single numeric feature is strongly correlated with the target (largest: procurement value, ρ ≈ 0.18) — failure is driven by combinations of factors (value × method × competition), which motivates a multivariate model rather than a single rule. The competition features form a tightly linked block: n_applications and n_bidders are identical in rank (ρ = 1.00 — one application per bidder), bids_per_lot is almost the same (ρ = 0.97), and more bidders go together with deeper discounts (best_bid_ratio, ρ = −0.71). has_parent is essentially a marker of single-source purchases (95 % of procurements with a parent link use that method). n_applications is therefore dropped from the feature set, and the remaining collinearity has to be kept in mind when reading linear-model coefficients.

9. Features (X), target (y) and data-leakage audit¶

Prediction moment. The model is meant to be used right after the winner is selected — when the procurement, its lots and all offers are known, but the contract has not been executed yet.

Target y = contract_failed. 1 if any contract that resulted from the procurement ended (last version of the contract chain) with status Terminated unilaterally (340), Terminated by mutual agreement (350), Not concluded (330), Awaiting termination (345) or their "transferred" variants (462, 463); 0 if all its contracts were executed, are active or amended without termination. Partially executed (375, 3.2 %) is ambiguous and is kept as 0; a strict target (without terminations by agreement, 4.5 %) is stored for sensitivity analysis.

Why this target: it is an observed, independently recorded event with a direct cost for the state. The earlier engineering prototype (Tender Radar) labelled "risk" with 31 hand-written rules; training a model on such labels only teaches it to reproduce the rules (circular). Here the rules' ideas enter as features, and the outcome is real.

lot_names (concatenated lot names) is kept in the table for the text branch of the project (TF-IDF in the midterm, transformer fine-tuning in A3). It is catalogue-like text: only ≈2–3 % of lot names are unique, so it behaves like a high-cardinality "what is bought" category.

9.1 Data-leakage audit¶

Candidate information Known at prediction time? Decision
Contract status, faktSum, faktExecDate, contractEndDate no — this is the outcome used only to build y
signDate, contractSum partly — set at signing; missing exactly for not-concluded contracts excluded (missingness reveals the label)
trd_buy.refBuyStatusId (procurement status) final state, may be updated after the contract fails excluded
itogiDatePublic (results date) may be re-published after the winner refuses to sign excluded
lastUpdateDate, indexDate system timestamps updated long after the award excluded
RNU register (supplier blacklisted) inclusion happens after termination (§5.5) excluded — consequence of the outcome
Past failure rate of the organiser / supplier would need outcomes of earlier contracts that were still running excluded; only activity counts (org_prior_buys) from publication dates
Imputation / scaling statistics computed on the full table they would leak fitted on the training split only (pipeline, §11)

assert not leaky & set(X_COLS), "a leaking column slipped into the features"

10. Train / validation / test split¶

The data are time-ordered, and the model will always be applied to future procurements, so the split is chronological — no random shuffling. A random split would let the model see procurements of the same weeks, organisers and market prices in training and testing, and would overestimate its quality.

Split Publication period Role
train 1 Jan – 29 Feb 2024 fit the model
validation 1 – 15 Mar 2024 choose model / threshold
test 16 – 31 Mar 2024 final, untouched evaluation

Calendar boundaries keep the split interpretable; they give ≈ 74 / 15 / 11 %, close to the usual 70 / 15 / 15. Stratification is not used — it would require shuffling across time; instead we check below that the positive rate is practically the same in every split (Figure 7 already showed no drift).

In [31]:

                                  first=("publish_dt", "min"), last=("publish_dt", "max")).loc[["train", "val", "test"]]
summary["share"] = summary.rows / summary.rows.sum()
assert summary["last"].iloc[0] < summary["first"].iloc[1] and summary["last"].iloc[1] < summary["first"].iloc[2]

11. Baseline model¶

A first reference point for the midterm: a majority/prior classifier (what we get without any model) and a logistic regression with class weighting. All preprocessing (median imputation with missing-indicators, scaling, one-hot encoding) is inside a scikit-learn Pipeline, so it is fitted on the training split only.

In [33]:
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, f1_score, precision_recall_curve, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

tr, va, te = (df[df.split == s] for s in ("train", "val", "test"))
pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True), StandardScaler()), NUM),
    ("bin", "passthrough", BIN),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", min_frequency=50), CAT),
])
logreg = make_pipeline(pre, LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", max_iter=2000))
logreg.fit(tr[X_COLS], tr[TARGET])
dummy = DummyClassifier(strategy="prior").fit(tr[X_COLS], tr[TARGET])

# decision threshold chosen on validation (max F1), then applied unchanged to test
p_val = logreg.predict_proba(va[X_COLS])[:, 1]
prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(va[TARGET], p_val)
threshold = thr[np.argmax((2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec + 1e-12))[:-1])]

def evaluate(model, part, name):
    p = model.predict_proba(part[X_COLS])[:, 1]
    top = np.argsort(-p)[: int(len(p) * 0.01)]
    return {"model": name, "ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(part[TARGET], p),
            "PR-AUC": average_precision_score(part[TARGET], p),
            "F1": f1_score(part[TARGET], p >= threshold) if name.startswith("Logistic") else 0.0,
            "precision@top1%": part[TARGET].iloc[top].mean(), "base rate": part[TARGET].mean()}

res = pd.DataFrame([evaluate(m, part, f"{n} — {s}") for s, part in (("validation", va), ("test", te))
                    for n, m in (("Prior (no model)", dummy), ("Logistic regression", logreg))])
print(f"decision threshold (tuned on validation): {threshold:.3f}")
res.round(3)

decision threshold (tuned on validation): 0.715

Baseline result. On the untouched test period (16–31 March) the logistic regression reaches ROC-AUC ≈ 0.79 and PR-AUC ≈ 0.27 — about four times the base rate of 6.6 % — while the prior classifier has ROC-AUC 0.5 by construction. Among the 1 % of procurements the model ranks as most risky, more than half actually failed (≈ 7.6× the base rate). Validation and test scores are close, so the model is not overfitted to a particular period. The coefficients (Figure 9) agree with the EDA: the request-for-quotations method, procurement value and the absence of recorded offers increase the risk; framework-agreement call-offs, scoring-system tenders and services/works (compared with goods) decrease it. The opposite signs of n_bidders (+) and bids_per_lot (−) are a symptom of their collinearity (Observation 8) and of the U-shaped effect that a linear term cannot represent — a concrete argument for the tree-based models planned for the midterm, together with the text of lot names.

12. Scientific interpretation and conclusions¶

RQ1 — method and competition. The procurement method is one of the strongest factors: automatic lowest-price requests for quotations fail about three times as often as single-source purchases and seven times as often as framework call-offs. H1 is supported, but only after controlling for the method: naively, single-bidder procurements look safest (Simpson's paradox), yet within the same method one bidder is riskier than two or three. The relationship with competition is U-shaped — very intense competition (6+ bidders) is risky again, consistent with the winner's curse in lowest-price auctions. For practice this means that "single bidder" — the most popular red flag in the procurement-integrity literature — should be interpreted relative to the method, and that extreme price competition deserves equal attention.

RQ2 — size, type, location. H2 is supported: the failure rate grows tenfold from the cheapest to the most expensive decile. Goods fail twice as often as services, and the three largest cities have about twice the failure rate of several regions. Value, subject and region are therefore informative, and an auditor's limited capacity should naturally be weighted towards large, goods-type, big-city procurements.

RQ3 — predictability. H3 is supported: a simple logistic regression trained on January–February ranks March procurements with ROC-AUC ≈ 0.79 and a PR-AUC four times the base rate, and half of its top-1 % list are real failures. Information available at award time is thus genuinely predictive of contract failure.

Limitations.

  1. One quarter of one year: seasonality (e.g. year-end purchases) is not represented.
  2. The label mixes failures caused by suppliers and decisions of customers (termination by agreement); the strict variant is stored for a sensitivity check.
  3. Supplier and organiser track records cannot be used without leakage because the outcome dates of earlier contracts are not observed; the RNU register is a consequence of failure, not a predictor.
  4. Offers are missing for some procurements (16 % without priced offers) and price units are occasionally inconsistent.
  5. The analysis is associational — the observed effects (e.g. of the method) are not causal.

Next steps (midterm / A3). Tree-based models (Random Forest, gradient boosting) to capture the interactions found in the EDA (value × method × competition); TF-IDF and a fine-tuned multilingual transformer on lot names; threshold and calibration analysis; comparison with the 31 rule-based indicators of the earlier Tender Radar prototype.
